lectures.title: Statutory bodies: meaning, examples and the Lokpal

items: **Statutory Body:** Created by an Act of Parliament or State Legislature (e.g., NHRC, Lokpal, NGT).
**Universities Grants Commission Act (1956):** Purpose: higher education regulation.
**Zonal Councils vs Inter-State Council:** Zonal Councils are Statutory Bodies created under Section 15 of the States Reorganisation Act, 1956 (Home Minister is the common Chairman).
**NHRC Trap:** Options pairing NHRC with an Article are FALSE (NHRC is a statutory body under the 1993 Act).

parts.t: Ombudsman, Lokpal and Lokayukta: the firsts
items: **Ombudsman:** Institution of Ombudsman first created in Sweden (1809).
**First Administrative Reforms Commission (1966):** recommended Lokpal & Lokayuktas (interim report by Morarji Desai).
**First Lokpal of India:** Justice Pinaki Chandra Ghose.
**Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act:** 2013 (came into effect in 2014).
**Coverage:** covers PM and public servants inside/outside India.
**5-member Selection Committee:** Prime Minister (Chairperson), Speaker (LS), LoP (LS), CJI/SC Judge nominee, Eminent Jurist.
**Trap:** Rajya Sabha Chairman is NOT a member of the Lokpal Selection Committee.
**Core Nature:** Quasi-judicial, specialized dispute resolution bodies created to reduce pendency in regular courts and provide domain expertise.
**Insertion:** Part XIV-A was inserted by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976 on the recommendations of the Swaran Singh Committee.
**Part Number Misattribution:** Any option placing Tribunals in Part XI (Relations between Union and States) or Part X (Scheduled & Tribal Areas) is FALSE - It is strictly Part XIV-A.
Exclusively covers public service matters (recruitment & conditions of service of Union, State, local/statutory authority employees)
Covers a specified list of other specialized subjects (list below)
Created ONLY by Parliament by law (Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985)
Created by both Parliament and State Legislatures (within their respective legislative competence)
Only one Central Administrative Tribunal (CAT) and State Administrative Tribunals (SATs) per State / Joint
A hierarchy of tribunals can be created
**Subjects under Article 323-B:** Taxation, Foreign Exchange, Industrial Disputes, Land Reforms, Ceiling on Property, Foodstuffs, Elections to Parliament/State Legislatures.

**Enactment Power Distinction:** State Legislatures have NO power to enact laws under Article 323-A (vested exclusively in Parliament); they CAN enact tribunal laws under Article 323-B on subjects within their legislative competence.
L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India, 1997 (Judicial Review Anchor)

**Basic Structure:** The Supreme Court held that the power of judicial review of the High Courts under Article 226/227 and the Supreme Court under Article 32 is an integral part of the Basic Structure.
**Exclusion clauses:** Clauses excluding the jurisdiction of High Courts and the Supreme Court in Articles 323-A and 323-B were declared unconstitutional.
**Route:** Decisions of tribunals (like CAT) are subject to scrutiny before a Division Bench of the concerned High Court before approaching the Supreme Court.

**Article 227(4):** High Court's superintendence under Article 227 does NOT extend to courts and tribunals constituted under laws relating to the Armed Forces (Art. 227(4) / Armed Forces Tribunal Act, 2007).
**Established:** in 1985 under the Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985 (Article 323-A).
**Jurisdiction:** Has original jurisdiction over service matters of civil servants under the Union.
**Appeals:** Appeals against CAT orders lie before the Division Bench of the jurisdictional High Court (L. Chandra Kumar rule).

parts.t: Telecom Disputes Settlement and Appellate Tribunal (TDSAT)
items: **Established:** under the TRAI (Amendment) Act, 2000 (Original parent act: TRAI Act, 1997).
**Work:** Adjudicates disputes in telecom, broadcasting, and airport tariff matters.
**Appellate Routes:** Telecom/broadcasting/tariff appeals lie directly to the Supreme Court on substantial questions of law; cyber appellate orders route to the High Court.
**National Green Tribunal (NGT) Act:** 2010; the NGT is a statutory body established under the National Green Tribunal Act, 2010.
**Procedure:** Guided by principles of Natural Justice, not bound by the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908.
**Appeals:** Appeals against NGT orders lie directly to the Supreme Court (within 90 days).
**Illegal Migrants (Determination by Tribunals) Act [IMDT Act, 1983]:** Struck down as unconstitutional by the Supreme Court in Sarbananda Sonowal v. Union of India (2005).
**Ground:** it violated Article 355 (Duty of the Union to protect States against external aggression and internal disturbance).
